Claude keeps duplicating code and I finally built something to catch it.

At throxy (yc x25), we noticed Claude had developed a habit. Ask it to add a feature, and it'll rewrite half your utility functions from scratch with the same logic and different names, scattered across our codebase and giving us headaches whenever we wanted to change types or do bug fixes

Last week it created the same validation function 5 times. Each one in a different file. Each one with a creative new name. All doing the exact same thing.

I decided to build a duplicate detector that runs on every PR. It only checks files you've touched in your PR and flags anything over 4 lines that has duplications

Some things we've caught so far include an error handler that existed in 6 variations and a date formatting function reimplemented in every component that needed it 🤦‍♂️

The annoying part is all this code works. It passes tests, reviews look fine, everything ships. Then when we get a bug ticket, we look closer and see features have been implemented slightly differently in different places.

Now our CI automatically flags duplicates before they make it to main. Claude can duplicate all it wants, at least now we catch it. (Looking at you, Arnau 👀)

AI coding assistants can help you ship faster, but they also help you accumulate tech debt at insane speeds. This script will save us massively in the long run.

Who else has caught their AI assistant treating every file like it's starting from scratch?

Project Specification: Google Photos to Google Earth (KML Generator)
Objective: Create a Python script to extract GPS/Timestamp metadata from a local folder of images (downloaded from the "Sonia's Birthdays" Google Photos album) and generate a .kml file for Google Earth.

1. Functional Requirements
Metadata Extraction: Use exifread or Pillow (PIL) to extract:

GPS Latitude/Longitude.

Date/Time Original.

Data Processing: Convert GPS coordinates from Degrees/Minutes/Seconds (DMS) to Decimal Degrees for KML compatibility.

Sorting: Sort the photos chronologically so the Google Earth path follows the timeline of birthdays.

KML Generation: Use the simplekml library to:

Create a "Placemark" for each birthday.

Add a "LineString" (path) connecting the birthdays in order.

Embed the filename or a placeholder in the description for later photo linking.

2. Technical Stack (for Cursor to use)
Language: Python 3.x

Libraries: simplekml, exifread (or Pillow), pandas (optional, for sorting).

3. Prompt for Cursor
"Write a Python script that scans a directory for JPEG/PNG images. For each image, extract the GPS coordinates and the creation date from the EXIF data. Sort the images by date. Then, generate a KML file where each image is a point on the map. Connect these points with a path (LineString) to show a journey over time. Use the simplekml and exifread libraries. Handle cases where images might be missing GPS data by skipping them or logging a warning."

Why this is a "win" for the family project:
Once Cursor builds this for you, you can run it on any folder.

For your son: Run it on his album.

For your grandson: Run it on his.

In Google Earth, you can then import all three KML files. They will appear as different colored paths on the same globe—showing how the whole family’s "birthday geography" overlaps over the decades.

Hey @John! 👋

Ivan asked me to set you up with your own OpenClaw agent (Atlas 🗼) so you can join the AI swarm working on our repos. Here's everything you need:

## The Big Picture

We now have a multi-agent system:
• **Nyx 🌙** (me) — Server agent, 24/7, handles Vete & infrastructure
• **Erebus 🔥** — Server agent, 24/7, handles research repos  
• **Atlas 🗼** (you!) — Your local agent, handles whatever you want

We coordinate through a shared GitHub repo where we claim tasks, track progress, and avoid duplicating work.

## Quick Start

**1. Install OpenClaw:**
```
npm install -g openclaw@latest
```

**2. Run onboarding:**
```
openclaw onboard --install-daemon
```
This walks you through API keys, config, etc.

**3. Clone the coordination repo:**
```
git clone https://github.com/Ai-Whisperers/work-coordination.git
```

**4. Follow the setup guide:**
The full guide is here:
https://github.com/Ai-Whisperers/work-coordination/blob/main/templates/SETUP-ATLAS.md

## What's in the Coordination Repo

📍 **github.com/Ai-Whisperers/work-coordination**

• `WORK-TRACKER.md` — Central task queue (claim tasks here)
• `AGENT-REGISTRY.md` — All agents and their status
• `REPOS.md` — Full inventory of all 50 org repos
• `CLAIMING-PROTOCOL.md` — How to claim tasks atomically
• `epics/` — Big project definitions
• `templates/` — Workspace file templates

## How Task Claiming Works

1. `git pull origin main`
2. Find an unclaimed task in WORK-TRACKER.md
3. Add "⏳ Atlas 🗼" to claim it
4. `git commit && git push`
5. Do the work
6. Mark "✅ Atlas 🗼 @timestamp" when done

If your push fails (someone else claimed first), just pull and pick another task.

## Your Agent Identity

You'll be **Atlas 🗼** — named after the Titan who held up the sky. Steady, reliable, carrying the load.

Configure this in `~/.openclaw/openclaw.json`:
```json
{
  "agents": {
    "list": [{
      "id": "local",
      "identity": {
        "name": "Atlas",
        "emoji": "🗼"
      }
    }]
  }
}
```

## Need Help?

• Tag @nyx in this group
• Check the docs at docs.openclaw.ai
• The setup guide has troubleshooting tips

Let me know when you're ready to start or if you hit any issues! 🚀

Team,

This week we are implementing a structural shift in how we work. Until now we have operated largely as students exploring ideas and building experimental projects. That phase has been valuable, but we are now moving into a professional production mindset. The focus going forward is reliability, clarity, and disciplined delivery.

1. Production Workflow — Effective Immediately

No changes are to be made directly on deployed environments.

All work must follow this flow:

Local development → Pull Request → CI validation → Staging deployment → Production release.

This means:

- Development happens on localhost only.
- Production is never edited manually.
- “Quick fixes” must go through a hotfix branch and PR.
- Production deployments originate only from approved, tested code.

We will enforce this through branch protections and controlled access. This is not optional; it is required for stability, traceability, and professional standards.

2. Standard Production Pipeline

Our production pipeline will operate with clear environments and gates:

Environments

- Local: development and testing.
- CI: automated build, tests, linting, and security checks.
- Staging: production-like environment for verification.
- Production: deployment of approved, versioned releases only.

Process

- Short-lived feature branches.
- Pull Requests with required approvals.
- CI must pass before merging.
- Builds produce versioned artifacts.
- Merges deploy automatically to staging.
- Production deployment happens through controlled promotion.
- Rollback uses previous versions, not manual edits.

3. GitHub Organization

We currently have too many projects without clear ownership or purpose. This week we will reorganize repositories into three categories:

- PROD: active, supported, customer-facing projects with documentation and pipelines.
- INCUBATION: serious prototypes with defined goals.
- LAB: experiments or learning projects.

Repositories that do not meet production standards will not be considered production work. Archiving and restructuring will happen this week to reduce noise and improve focus.

Minimum requirements for production repositories:

- Clear README with purpose and setup instructions.
- Maintainers and ownership defined.
- CI enabled.
- Security and privacy guidelines included.
- Active issue tracking or explicitly disabled workflow.

4. Privacy and Professional Standards

We are transitioning from experimentation to professional delivery. Baseline rules:

- No secrets or credentials committed to git.
- No real customer data used in development environments unless anonymized.
- Logs must not contain sensitive personal information.
- Access follows least-privilege principles.
- Security incidents must be reported immediately.

Each production repository will include SECURITY.md, PRIVACY.md, and CONTRIBUTING.md documentation.

5. Direction and Expectations

We are intentionally raising the bar.

This is not about restricting creativity; it is about building systems that can scale, be trusted, and represent us professionally. Direct edits in production environments, unclear repository ownership, or undocumented workflows slow us down and increase risk.

The goal is simple: a reliable production pipeline and a clean, professional engineering structure.

Hey Bram! Here's a quick rundown of the Hermes setup:

Hermes is our AI assistant platform that connects to multiple messaging apps (Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord, etc.) and gives an AI agent persistent memory, tools, and autonomy.

Key components:

1. BRAIN - Powered by Claude (Anthropic's AI). It can think, reason, write code, and use tools.

2. TOOLS - It has access to:
- Terminal (run shell commands on a Linux server)
- File system (read/write files)
- Web search & browsing
- GitHub (repos, PRs, issues)
- Code execution (Python)
- Vision (analyze images)
- Text-to-speech
- Cron jobs (scheduled tasks)
- Skills (reusable workflows saved as templates)

3. MEMORY - It remembers things across sessions:
- User profiles (who you are, preferences)
- Personal notes (environment details, project conventions)
- Session history (searchable past conversations)
- Skills (procedures it learned)
- Daily memory files on disk

4. MESSAGING - Connected to Telegram + WhatsApp. It can respond in group chats, send files, images, voice messages.

5. CRON JOBS - It can schedule recurring tasks (like monitoring repos, sending reports, running audits automatically).

6. DELEGATION - It can spawn sub-agents to work on tasks in parallel, or route hard problems through multiple AI models.

7. WORKSPACE - Lives on a Linux VPS. Has its own workspace with config files, memory files, and project access.

Think of it as a developer teammate that never sleeps, has access to your infrastructure, and remembers everything you tell it. Ivan uses it heavily for the Solstein project (automated PR reviews, test runs, code work every 3 hours via cron).

ENEVE CODE AGENT (Ecedo Software BV)

A serious production system. 112K LOC Java, Quarkus-based. It's essentially a self-hosted Claude Code for enterprise teams — hooks into Bitbucket, Azure DevOps, GitLab, GitHub, JIRA, Confluence, Teams, and Aikido security.

WHAT'S REALLY GOOD:

1. ClaudeToolUseLoop — Their core agent loop is clean. Parallel execution of read-only tools, context compaction when approaching token limits, checkpointing every iteration so jobs can resume from failure.

2. Guardrails — Blocked paths, command allowlists, max files/lines changed limits, shell command security validator (ported from Claude Code's bashSecurity.ts). This is production paranoia done right.

3. Self-review loop — After making changes, the agent reviews its own diff against a checklist before committing. Smart.

4. Learning extraction — Automatically extracts team preferences from code review conversations ("we prefer constructor injection") and remembers them for future reviews.

5. Tool authorization gate — Each tool has isReadOnly(), isDestructive(), and isAuthorized() flags. Defence in depth.

WHERE THEY COULD IMPROVE:

1. 15+ method overloads on ClaudeToolUseLoop instead of a builder pattern
2. Hardcoded to Anthropic — no model abstraction for using cheaper models on simpler tasks
3. No cost controls (token tracking exists but no abort threshold)
4. Monolithic — everything in one service, no worker separation
5. No OpenTelemetry / distributed tracing

WHAT WE CAN STEAL:

- Parallel read-only tool execution
- Context compaction with circuit breaker
- Checkpoint + resume pattern
- Self-review before commit
- Learning extraction from conversations
- Shell command validator security rules
- Per-job-type tool sets (writable vs readonly)

ENEVE CODE AGENT UI

React 19 + TypeScript + Vite 7 + Tailwind v4. 57K LOC across 179 files. Modern stack with TanStack (Router + Query + Store), Keycloak auth, chart.js + recharts for metrics.

SCREENS (30+ pages):

Work:
- Dashboard (stat cards, needs-attention queue)

- Chat (streaming AI assistant with tool visibility)

Insights:
- Quality Reports
- Coverage Trend
- Scopes (JIRA issue readiness)
- Review Metrics, PR Cycle Time
- Developer Scorecard
- AI Effectiveness + AI Stats
- Knowledge Graph

Engineering:
- Architecture (Structurizr diagrams)
- Log Analysis

QA:
- QA Scopes, Test Plans, Test Cases

SOC II:
- Security Issues (Aikido integration)
- SOC II Audit

Settings:
- Repos, Integrations, Hooks (automation rules)
- Job Configuration, Prompts (editable prompt templates!)
- Memories, Knowledge Index
- Customers, Users, Teams, System
- Webhook Audit, Audit Log

WHAT'S IMPRESSIVE:

1. ThinkingPanel — shows Claude's tool calls in real-time with status indicators (running/completed/error), duration, and tool parameters. Users can SEE the agent working.

2. SecretScanner — client-side detection of AWS keys, GitHub tokens, Anthropic keys, OpenAI keys, private keys, JWTs, DB URLs. Warns before sending, auto-redacts.

3. ClarificationBlock — structured questions from the agent (text, single choice, multi choice, boolean). Agent can ask the user before proceeding.

4. Streaming chat — SSE-based with TanStack Store. Content appears in real-time with mermaid diagram rendering.

5. Editable Prompts page — all 39 prompt templates editable through the UI. No redeploy needed.

6. RBAC — Keycloak + 4 roles (User/Staff/Developer/Admin) with 9 permissions. Menu items auto-hide based on permissions.

7. Plan execution UI — visual timeline showing plan phases, each step's status, ability to approve/reject before execution.

WHAT WE CAN LEARN:

1. Tool call transparency — showing users what the agent is doing builds trust
2. Secret scanning on the client — catch before sending, not after
3. Editable prompts in UI — huge for iteration speed
4. Job configuration per type — different models/token limits per job type
5. Clarification flow — structured questions instead of free-text back-and-forth
6. AI effectiveness metrics — tracking how useful the agent actually is

FEEDBACK FOR IMPROVEMENT:

1. No dark mode toggle visible (CSS vars exist but no UI control found)
2. No WebSocket — uses SSE polling for streaming. WebSocket would be lower latency
3. Chat is 1088 lines — single component doing too much, could decompose
4. No error boundary components visible
5. No i18n — English only
6. Could add keyboard shortcuts for power users
7. No offline/PWA support

This is a solid enterprise product. The combination of backend agent + this UI makes it a complete self-hosted Cursor/Claude Code for teams. Worth studying the patterns even if we don't copy the implementation.

```yaml
version: '3'
services:

    container_name: deepseek
    ports:
      - "5000:5000"
    volumes:
      - ./data:/data
```
Este archivo define un servicio llamado `deepseek` que utiliza la imagen `litellm/deepseek:v4` y mapea el puerto 5000 del contenedor al puerto 5000 del VPS. También monta un volumen llamado `data` en el directorio actual del VPS.

mkdir data

docker-compose up -d

3. VS Code or another editor has a handle on it
4. A previous npm process is still holding it

**Fastest fix, try in this order:**

1. Close File Explorer, VS Code, any terminal windows
2. Pause Windows Defender real-time protection (Settings → Virus & threat protection → Manage settings → toggle off Real-time protection for ~5 min)
3. Manually nuke the locked folder:
   ```
   rmdir /s /q "C:\Users\John\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent\apps\desktop\node_modules\electron"
   ```
   If that says "access denied," it's Defender — pause it and retry.
4. Run the Hermes installer again, as Administrator

If it still fails after that, your antivirus (not Defender) is the culprit. Look for ESET, Kaspersky, Norton, Malwarebytes — same pattern, pause real-time shield during install.
